Eyeball 2

GeometryCirclesConstructions
What it shows: Two circles, straight lines touching them, and a small green circle inside each one.
How to play: Drag the four dots, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Move the circles and their rims to see what changes and what stays the same.
Look for the math

Move the dots and the two green circles grow or shrink together. What looks like a free choice of sizes is really one formula with the two circles swapped.

Four touching lines

Let the circles have centres A, B, radii RA, RB, and centre distance AB. The dot P is the point of the first circle farthest from B, and Q is the point of the second farthest from A. From each of these points two tangent lines touch the other circle. The lines and the arc between them make the two curved, "isosceles" triangles. The drawing works exactly when neither circle swallows the other's far point: AB > |RA − RB|. The logic test checks that boundary across thousands of configurations.

One radius from similar triangles

For the tangent line PT, the radius BT is perpendicular to it, so PTB is a right triangle with PB = RA + AB and BT = RB. The green incircle of the curved triangle touches the same line at S; its centre R lies PR = 2RA − RS from P, because the little circle touches the big one at the point facing the other circle. The two right triangles are similar, so

PB / BT = PR / RS
(RA + AB) / RB = (2RA − RS) / RS
RS = 2 RA RB / (RA + RB + AB)

Why the two circles match

The formula is unchanged when A and B are swapped, and swapping them is exactly how the second curved triangle is made. So its circle has the same radius. This is the page's exact claim — the two "incircles" are always equal — and the logic test confirms it, including that each green circle really touches its two tangent lines and its own circle from the inside. It also confirms that when AB < |RA − RB| there are no tangents at all, so the claim is only about the drawable cases. This differs from the sibling Eyeball applet, whose single orange circle has radius AB/2 at the midpoint of the centres; the two theorems are not the same statement.

An old tablet, and a small quirk

The page calls this an 1842 sangaku from Aichi prefecture. Its live page now embeds a GeoGebra picture instead of the Java applet; the 2012 archived page does embed APPLET CODE="Eyeball2". One quirk: the Java code places its two green circles at the outer points P and Q, touching their own circles there, while the page's diagram and proof place them on the sides facing each other, touching the tangents. Both placements use the same radius, which is what the theorem asserts; this port follows the page's diagram.

Try moving a rim dot until one circle nearly contains the other: the tangents disappear just as the green radius would outgrow the smaller circle.
